title: Agent Behavioral Contracts: Formal Specification and Runtime Enforcement for Reliable Autonomous AI Agents
tldr: Introduces Agent Behavioral Contracts (ABC), a formal framework with runtime enforcement that bounds behavioral drift and achieves 88-100% compliance in autonomous AI agents.
problem_and_motivation: AI agents operate without formal behavioral guarantees, relying instead on natural language prompts that carry no verifiable enforcement mechanisms. This gap causes behavioral drift, governance failures, and silent degradation in multi-turn agent interactions. Traditional software contracts and existing safety approaches like Constitutional AI and RLHF cannot enforce deployment-specific constraints at runtime.
approach: Defined ABC contract structure C = (P,I,G,R) specifying preconditions, invariants, governance policies, and recovery mechanisms.
Introduced (p,δ,k)-satisfaction, a probabilistic compliance framework accounting for LLM non-determinism and bounded recovery.
Proved Drift Bounds Theorem using Lyapunov stability analysis showing contracts bound drift to D* = α/γ when recovery rate exceeds natural drift.
Implemented AgentAssert runtime enforcement library with sub-10ms per-action overhead for contract evaluation.
Evaluated on AgentContract-Bench with 200 scenarios across 7 models from 6 vendors over 1,980 sessions.
findings: num: Contracted agents detect 5.2-6.8 soft violations per session that uncontracted baselines miss entirely.
num: 88-100% hard constraint compliance achieved across all tested models.
num: Behavioral drift bounded to D* < 0.27 across extended sessions.
num: 100% recovery success for frontier models, 17-100% across all models.
num: Runtime enforcement overhead less than 10ms per action.
num: Statistical significance achieved with p < 0.0001 and Cohen's d = 6.7-33.8.
Recovery mechanisms transform exponential compliance decay into linear decay.
Compositionality theorem provides sufficient conditions for multi-agent contract composition.

definitions.definition: Agent Behavioral Contracts - formal framework bringing Design-by-Contract principles to autonomous AI agents.
Probabilistic contract compliance where p is probability threshold, δ is tolerance, k is recovery window.
Progressive divergence of agent behavior from intended specifications over extended interactions.
Two-component metric combining compliance-gap and Jensen-Shannon divergence as diagnostic and predictive signal.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper formalizes agent behavioral contracts as a runtime-enforceable framework with probabilistic guarantees. It introduces the (p,δ,k)-satisfaction definition that accounts for LLM non-determinism and bounded recovery windows. The Drift Bounds Theorem proves that contracts with adequate recovery rate bound behavioral drift in expectation. The compositionality theorem establishes conditions under which individual contracts compose into end-to-end guarantees for multi-agent chains. The work provides both theoretical foundations and practical implementation through the AgentAssert enforcement library.
directly_justifies: Contracted agents detect 5.2-6.8 soft violations per session that uncontracted baselines miss entirely.
Recovery mechanisms transform exponential compliance decay into linear decay.

Compositionality theorem enables contract composition across multi-agent pipelines.
Runtime enforcement overhead remains below 10ms per action.
limits: Evaluation limited to 7 models from 6 vendors, may not generalize to all LLM architectures.
Contract specification requires manual authoring by domain experts.
Recovery mechanisms are model-dependent, with 17-100% success across tested models.
Compositionality theorem assumes conditional independence between agents.
No formal verification of contract specifications themselves.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: All 14 topic domains were systematically scanned. Domain 4 (Landscape of Existing Systems) received high relevance for its comprehensive review of existing agent safety frameworks and identification of the formal contract gap. Domain 8 (Anomaly Detection) received medium relevance because behavioral drift detection functions as anomaly detection for agent behavior. Domain 12 (Evaluation Frameworks) received medium relevance for introducing new evaluation methodology. Domains 1-3 (Filipino Young Professionals, Financial Practices, Expense Categorization) were rejected as outside scope. Domain 5 (Financial Behavioral Profiles), Domain 6 (Predictive Modeling), Domain 7 (Budgeting), Domain 9 (Mobile-First Design), Domain 10 (Data Privacy), Domain 11 (Engagement), Domain 13 (Savings/Debt), and Domain 14 (Synthetic Data) were all rejected as they do not directly relate to the paper's focus on formal behavioral contracts for AI agents.
